Provisioning was a second subsystem with a separate interface and a separate backend, the network activator, used by operations staff. It booked appointments with carriers like CityFibre and Openreach. It drove activation of the optical network unit, the ONU, the device that terminates fibre at the premises. And it tracked network state as it moved from nothing, to provisioned, to configured. The portal interface owned the commercial order. The activator owned the physical line. They did not call each other synchronously. They stayed consistent through NATS, the messaging system, sending events, which is what let two halves built by different parts of the team evolve independently. The hard engineering was the external integrations. Carrier systems had their own contracts and identifier formats, and we validated those at our own boundary before a value could travel. A concrete example is the carrier appointment identifier. It had a fixed structured shape enforced by a validate-regex directive on the GraphQL, the graph query language, input, so a malformed identifier was rejected at the edge with a specific message rather than failing opaquely hours later inside a carrier call. Pricing fields were validated the same way. A monthly price field carried a validate-regex with the pattern for a value between zero point zero zero and nine hundred and ninety nine point zero zero, with a human-readable message, so the constraint lived in the schema next to the field rather than in a controller. Not every record began as a firm order. A prospect was a softer, earlier entity. It had a create, read, update and delete surface and a permission set of its own. It was convertible into a subscriber and an order. And it had seeded templates and explicit not-found handling, so that an absent prospect was a defined state rather than an error. Batch orders created many service orders together. They needed dedicated seeded test data and dedicated validation, so a single bad row did not poison the batch. The order domain was therefore not one workflow but a family, prospect, single order, batch, regrade, suspend, resume, terminate, each a separate mutation with separate directives, sharing entity types generated from one GraphQL schema. Keeping that family consistent as the schema changed was exactly what schema-first code generation existed to make safe, because a change to a shared input type recompiled every consumer of it at once. It is worth being concrete about how a transition was actually shaped in code. A regrade was not a flag flip. It was a GraphQL mutation with a dedicated input type, dedicated validate and validate-regex directives on that input, a has-permission requirement naming the regrade permission, and a resolver method on the mutation resolver interface that the compiler forced to exist. The order entity carried a status modelled as a generated enumeration rather than a free string, so an impossible status could not be assigned because it was not a member of the type. Side effects were explicit. A successful transition published a protocol buffer event on a named subject, and the activation side consumed it rather than the portal calling the activator inline, so a slow carrier interaction could not block the commercial mutation. The carrier identifiers that crossed our boundary, the appointment identifier in particular, were validated by a validate-regex directive whose pattern and message lived on the input field in the schema, so a malformed identifier failed at the edge with a precise message instead of failing deep inside a carrier call where the cause is expensive to recover. That is the texture of the whole domain, many small typed mutations, each carrying a declarative policy, sharing generated entity types.

## System shape and scale

The repository was a single pnpm and Turborepo monorepo, and the monorepo was a correctness decision, not only an ergonomic one. Because every cross-service contract was generated from a schema that lived in the same repository, one commit could change a contract and every Go and TypeScript consumer of it in the same review, and the build failed immediately if any consumer was now wrong. The backend was Go, roughly two hundred and forty thousand lines. The frontend was TypeScript and React, roughly eighty thousand lines. There were five Go services. The portal interface was by far the largest. It exposed the GraphQL, the graph query language, API, the application programming interface, consumed by the operator frontends. The network activator interface was a representational state transfer service on the Echo web framework for operations workflows. The addressing service was a gRPC service, gRPC being the remote procedure call framework, backed by PostgreSQL rather than the document store used elsewhere. The tenancy service was a deliberately small broker for per-tenant connection and key material. The collateral service handled document storage in object storage. The frontend workspace had shared packages under a cortex scope, a validations package, a hooks package, a user interface package, a utilities package, and a constants package, so a rule like a valid United Kingdom phone number or an error-code enumeration had exactly one implementation imported by both the operator portal and the network activator frontend rather than two that drift. Testing was concrete. There was an end-to-end suite on Playwright, the browser automation framework, exercising real journeys, create and activate a service, manage a subscriber, work a support ticket. There were Go fuzz tests feeding malformed input into parsers. There were integration tests that stood real dependencies up in containers, the document database, the messaging system, and the portal interface, and ran them together rather than against mocks. Continuous integration on GitLab was a sequence of independent gates rather than one test step. A container-image lint job ran only when a container definition changed. A static-analysis job ran the Go linter across the module. A test job ran the suite with the race detector enabled, the flag that turns latent data races into hard failures in the pipeline rather than into rare production corruption. A vulnerability scan walked the Go module graph and failed the pipeline on a known advisory in a transitive dependency, not only a direct one. A versioning job computed a semantic version automatically on the main branch from commit history, so a release number was derived rather than typed. The reason these numbers matter is not their size. It is that a codebase this large with more than one author only stays internally consistent if consistency is generated and enforced mechanically. Almost every contribution I will describe is an instance of that single idea, replacing something that humans had to remember with something the compiler, the directive middleware, the code generator, or the pipeline checked automatically, because at this scale anything that depends on memory is a defect waiting for a deadline. Each pipeline job caught a different class of defect, and merging meant every independent job had agreed, not that one reviewer felt confident. The frontend had the parallel discipline through the code generator and the type checker. The deeper point is that scale does not break a system through any single large mistake. It breaks through many small inconsistencies that no individual notices, so the only durable defence is to make each class of inconsistency impossible to express or impossible to merge, which is exactly what generated contracts and gated pipelines do.

## The GraphQL core

The portal interface was a Go service exposing one GraphQL, the graph query language, API generated with gqlgen, a schema-first GraphQL server library. The schema files generated an executable schema and typed resolver interfaces, split into a query resolver and a mutation resolver, so the compiler enforced that every schema field had a matching Go method with the right signature. The resolver root was a single struct used for dependency injection. It held the addressing client, the document persistence client, the tenancy client, the collateral client, the NATS, the messaging system, client, the CityFibre and Openreach carrier clients, the per-pool key provider used to verify tokens, and the status providers used for health and readiness. A resolver did real work by reaching through that struct, never by constructing its own dependencies, which made every resolver unit-testable by substituting the struct fields with mocks generated by the mock generator. The gqlgen configuration mapped custom scalars to concrete Go types deliberately. A file upload scalar mapped to a real upload type so a multipart upload was a typed value. The formatted-text scalar mapped to a sanitised hypertext type rather than a bare string, so a resolver could not accidentally store unsanitised markup. Errors were wrapped through a shared error package that preserved the underlying cause while attaching a stable code, so the frontend received a structured error with a code and a path rather than an opaque string, which is what later let the frontend bind a rejection to an exact form field. The data store was a document database, and this is where multi-tenant isolation was concretely implemented. A resolver did not open a database. It called the persistence client with the request context, and the persistence client resolved the correct per-tenant connection from that context. The tenant identity arrived as a claim in a verified token, was extracted into a metadata value, and was placed in context by middleware before any resolver ran. There was a metadata accessor, read from context, that returned the tenant identifier, the user identifier, and the caller's permissions together, from one trusted source, so isolation and authorization were always decided from the same value rather than from two systems that could disagree. The service was event-driven over NATS. After a mutation, a resolver published an event, for example a user-updated subject or a support-ticket-created subject, carrying a protocol buffer message, and other services subscribed rather than being called directly. Process startup was itself a contract. The service read configuration from the environment. It registered OpenTelemetry tracing so one request could be followed across the portal interface, into the addressing service, and back. It opened the remote procedure call and messaging clients. It established the messaging client with signature verification, so a forged event was rejected on consume. It configured the carrier client with mutual transport security and client certificates. It fetched and cached the public verification keys for every tenant pool, so a token from any tenant could be verified without a per-request network call. And only then did it serve traffic, over a transport with a strict minimum version. Each of those startup steps existed because production had at some point required it, and treating startup as part of the contract rather than as glue is part of why the system was operable. Two implementation details are worth naming because they are the kind a reviewer would probe. First, authentication was a gqlgen extension rather than ad hoc resolver code. An authentication check ran as a schema extension, with a small, explicit list of open resolvers, for example a manifest query, that were intentionally reachable without a token, declared in one place, so unauthenticated reach was an enumerated allowlist rather than an accident of a missing annotation. Second, the metadata that every resolver depended on was not pulled from headers in each resolver. It was constructed once by middleware from the verified token and stored in request context as a single value carrying the tenant identifier, the user identity, and the permission set, and resolvers read it through one accessor. That centralisation is why isolation and authorization could never disagree, they were two reads of one value. The resolver struct itself was the dependency-injection seam. Because every external dependency was a field on that struct, a resolver test substituted those fields with generated mocks and exercised real resolver logic without a network, which is why the resolver layer was both the place business rules lived and the place they were cheapest to test.

## The other services

The portal interface was the largest service, but the design judgement is clearest in how the other four differed from it on purpose. The network activator interface was a representational state transfer service built on the Echo web framework. Its handlers were generated from an OpenAPI specification through oapi-codegen, an OpenAPI code generator, so the handler interface and the request and response models were generated from the specification rather than written by hand, and the implementation only filled in the generated interface. It authenticated with the same token scheme as the portal. It resolved each tenant to a separate identity pool through a tenant map. And it placed the same metadata value, tenant, user, permissions, into request context, so the isolation model was identical even though the transport was different. It ran a status server exposing health and a metrics endpoint on a separate port. The addressing service was a gRPC service, gRPC being the remote procedure call framework, over a PostgreSQL relational store, and the database access was generated by sqlc, a typed SQL, structured query language, code generator. The configuration targeted the PostgreSQL engine through the pgx PostgreSQL driver. It emitted prepared queries. And it applied type overrides, so a database universally unique identifier mapped to a Go string and a timestamp-with-time-zone mapped to a Go time value. Each query was an annotated statement with a name and a cardinality annotation, for example a many-row address lookup by postcode, and sqlc generated a typed Go function for it. There was no stringly-typed query text anywhere in the service, and a query that did not match its schema failed at code generation rather than at runtime. One representative query was a postcode lookup that sorted addresses by natural numeric order using a regular-expression match on the leading digits of the building number, so that two came before ten rather than after it, which is the kind of correctness detail that only a typed, reviewed query layer keeps honest. Schema changes were numbered up-migrations applied in order, not manual edits. The tenancy service was intentionally minimal, a broker for per-tenant connection and key material, and there was a tracked task to remove it and fold its responsibility elsewhere, which is the correct posture toward infrastructure whose only job is to glue other things together. The collateral service stored uploaded and generated documents in object storage. The throughline is fitness for purpose under one generated contract discipline. GraphQL where many entities compose into operator views. Representational state transfer where the surface is procedural and operational. Remote procedure calls over a relational store where the data is highly relational and query-heavy and a real query planner with indexes is the right tool. None of these were chosen for uniformity, and none of them drifted, because every boundary between them was a generated contract checked by the build rather than a hand-written client that could fall out of sync. A few more specifics make the query layer concrete, because that is where the relational discipline shows. The configuration also set the option to emit pointer types for nullable columns, so a nullable database value became an optional Go value rather than a silent zero. The type overrides were deliberate, so call sites never juggled driver-specific types. Each query carried a cardinality annotation, one row, many rows, or execute, and the generator emitted exactly one typed Go function per query, so the set of database operations was a closed, reviewable list rather than strings assembled at runtime. The postcode lookup sorted by the leading numeric portion of the building number through a regular-expression match so that natural order held, and that correctness lives in a reviewed query file rather than in scattered comparison code. The network activator interface had the analogous discipline on the representational state transfer side, where the OpenAPI specification generated the Echo handler interface and the models, and a separate status server exposed health and metrics on its own port so liveness probing never contended with request traffic.

## Schema first development

Schema-first code generation is the single mechanism that explains how the codebase stayed consistent across two languages and five services, so it is worth describing as a concrete pipeline rather than a slogan. There was one generate target. It ran a fixed, dependency-ordered sequence of scripts. First the OpenAPI generation, turning the representational state transfer specifications into Go handler interfaces and models. Then the protocol buffer generation, turning the proto service and message definitions into Go message types and remote procedure call stubs. Then the SQL, structured query language, generation, turning annotated queries into typed Go functions. Then the GraphQL, the graph query language, fragment generation, precompiling shared field selections. Then gqlgen, turning the GraphQL schema into the Go executable schema and resolver interfaces. Then the frontend code generation, turning the same schema plus the operation documents into TypeScript types and typed React hooks. Then the mock generation, turning interfaces into test doubles, which has to run last because the interfaces must exist first. Then seed generation and formatting. The ordering is not arbitrary. Mocks depend on interfaces, the frontend depends on the GraphQL schema, and gqlgen can depend on protocol buffer models, so the sequence encodes a dependency graph. The discipline was that the generated output was committed and reviewed alongside the change. That sounds like noise until you consider the failure it removes. In a hand-synchronised system a backend field rename ships, the frontend keeps the old name, the code still compiles, the existing tests still pass, and a customer finds the bug weeks later. Here, the same rename regenerated a TypeScript type whose new shape failed to compile at every call site, and regenerated a Go resolver interface whose new signature failed to compile in the resolver, both on the author's machine, before review. The mismatch became a located compile error rather than a production incident. I leaned on this directly in my own work. Because the frontend types were generated from the same schema as the backend, form field names were derived from generated input types rather than typed as string literals, so a renamed schema field produced a compile error at every form that referenced it instead of a silent runtime no-op. The honest cost is real. You commit large generated files and you accept a slower generate-and-build cycle. The return is that an entire class of cross-language, cross-service integration mistake cannot occur, because the contract is the source and every consumer is mechanically derived from it. The one state strictly worse than no code generation is code generation that people bypass by editing generated output by hand, because then the contract lies, so a real part of maintaining this system was keeping the generated output authoritative and never hand-edited, which is unglamorous but is the property the whole architecture depends on. It helps to trace one schema change through the pipeline concretely. Suppose an input field on the update-subscriber input is renamed. The protocol buffer step is unaffected. The gqlgen step regenerates the Go model and the resolver interface, so the resolver method no longer satisfies the generated interface and the Go build fails at that method. The frontend code-generator step regenerates the TypeScript input type, so every form that referenced the old field name fails type checking at that exact property access. The fragment step regenerates any shared selection that named the field. Mock generation runs last and regenerates the interface mocks so tests compile against the new shape. One rename, several generated diffs, every one of them a compile error on the author's machine, none of them a runtime surprise. The plugins on the frontend side were the typescript plugin, the typescript-operations plugin, and the typescript-react-apollo plugin, which together produced a typed hook per operation with a typed variables object and a typed result, and the generator preserved enumeration value names rather than rewriting them so the generated enumerations matched the backend exactly. Because the field name in a form was read from that generated input type rather than written as a literal, the rename propagated into the validation layer too, which is the seam between this chapter and the validation framework chapter later.

## Authorization and input safety

Authorization and input validation were declarative GraphQL, the graph query language, directives enforced by middleware, not imperative checks inside resolvers, and that is the design decision with the highest security leverage in the system. There were four directives. The has-permission directive annotated a field with the permissions required to call it, written in a resource and action style, for example read on the order resource or update on the subscriber resource. It was wired into the gqlgen directive root, so before a protected resolver executed, the directive middleware compared the permissions on the request metadata against the permissions the field declared, and on mismatch returned an authorization error so the resolver never ran. Because the requirement lived in the schema next to the field, the entire access-control surface was readable as data rather than reconstructed from scattered conditionals. The validate directive applied struct-tag rules from the Go validator library to input fields, for example required, a universally unique identifier format, a maximum length of twenty-five, or a dive into a list to validate each element, each with an optional human-readable message. The validate-regex directive enforced a pattern with a message, which is how the carrier appointment identifier format and the monthly price format were rejected at the boundary. The html directive ran a field through the bluemonday HTML sanitiser with its user-generated-content policy, stripping dangerous markup to prevent cross-site scripting, which is the attack where attacker markup executes in another user's session. I did specific work on this surface. I added the safe formatted-text scalar and its directive, wiring it through the schema and the generated code so the type system carried the sanitisation guarantee, and I fixed a real defect where a trailing newline from a text area input slipped past a check, by trimming before validation. The authorization model had a small, explicit set of open resolvers, for example a manifest query, that were intentionally callable without authentication, declared in one place rather than implied by the absence of a directive, so unauthenticated access was an enumerated allowlist rather than a thing you could create by forgetting an annotation. The property that ties this chapter together is that a newly added resolver was secure by default. With no annotation it required authentication, exposed no data shape that bypassed validation, and could not store unsanitised markup, because the safe behaviours were the defaults enforced by middleware and the type system, and opening a field up required a visible, reviewable change to the schema rather than remembering to add a protection whose absence is invisible. Secure-if-you-remember fails under deadline pressure precisely when load is highest. Secure-by-default does not, which is why expressing the policy as schema directives rather than as resolver code was worth the cost of building the directive machinery. The wiring is worth stating precisely because it is the part an interviewer would push on. Each directive was registered in the gqlgen directive root, the structure that maps a schema directive name to a Go function the generated executable schema invokes around a field. The has-permission function received the field's declared permission list and the request, read the permission set from the metadata accessor, and either proceeded or returned an authorization error before the resolver function was ever called, so an unauthorized call did zero business work. The validate function constructed a validator from the Go validator library and applied the struct-tag rules carried by the directive, so a rule like a maximum length or a required identifier was data on the schema field, not a branch in a handler. The validate-regex function compiled the pattern from the directive and matched the input, returning the directive's message on failure. The html function ran the value through the sanitiser configured with the user-generated-content policy and returned the cleaned value, so sanitisation happened before the resolver saw the input rather than being a step a resolver author had to remember. Because all four were invoked by the generated schema rather than by resolver code, adding a resolver added zero security code and inherited every default, which is the entire point of putting policy in the schema.

## Multi tenant isolation

Multi-tenant isolation was implemented in context propagation and in physical data separation, and the implementation is specific enough to describe end to end. Every tenant was an internet service provider with a separate identity pool in a managed authentication service, so users were entirely separate per tenant with no shared accounts. A request arrived with a token. Middleware verified the token against the correct pool's public keys. The portal interface fetched and cached the verification keys for every pool at startup, and refreshed them, so verification never required a per-request call to the authentication provider. From the verified claims, middleware constructed a metadata value carrying the tenant identifier, the user identifier, and the caller's permissions, and placed it in the request context. There was a single accessor that read that metadata back out of context, and resolvers used it for both isolation and authorization, from the same trusted value, so the two decisions could not disagree. Data isolation was physical. There was no shared database with a tenant column. Each tenant had a separate document database. The persistence client took the request context and resolved the correct per-tenant connection from the tenant identifier in the metadata, and a resolver called the persistence client with context rather than ever choosing a database itself. The consequence is structural. A resolver cannot reach another tenant's data by forgetting a filter, because there is no shared collection in which a filter could have been forgotten. The one deliberate exception was the addressing service on PostgreSQL, where geographic and network data is genuinely common across tenants and per-tenant duplication would be wrong, and there isolation was enforced explicitly in the query layer, which is the correct approach when sharing is the examined choice rather than an accident. Provisioning a tenant was not merely creating an empty database. A new tenant needed a baseline, an administrator role with full permissions, an operator role, a narrower tenant-user role, the permissions attached to those roles, product offerings, order status values, and activity types, all present before the first order could exist. There was a seed generator that produced this baseline deterministically, and I did substantial work on it, attaching new resource permissions to the correct roles, seeding prospect and subscriber templates, and adding explicit not-found handling for absent prospects. The reason that boring layer matters is that every local environment, every continuous integration run, and every freshly provisioned tenant depends on the seed being correct and identical, so a wrong seed makes every downstream test confidently assert against the wrong world. Isolation is not one feature. It is a property the entire request path preserves, from key verification, through context construction, through connection resolution, and a single shortcut anywhere on that path breaks it everywhere. The metadata value deserves one more concrete pass because it is the spine of isolation. It was modelled as a protocol buffer message with fields for the tenant identifier, the creating user identity and name, the updating user identity and name, the timestamps, and the entity type. Modelling it as a proto message rather than an ad hoc struct meant the same tenancy and audit fields travelled identically whether they moved through request context inside a service or through a published event between services, so an event consumer saw the same tenant attribution the originating resolver had. The persistence client used the tenant identifier from that value to select the per-tenant connection, and it stamped the creating and updating identity onto written documents from the same value, so audit metadata and isolation were never two separate code paths that could diverge. The key provider closed the loop at the front. It fetched the verification keys for every tenant pool at startup and refreshed them, so token verification was a local operation, and a token issued by one tenant pool simply did not verify against another pool's keys, which means cross-tenant impersonation failed at verification rather than being caught later by a filter. Isolation, audit, and authentication therefore all derived from one verified value flowing through context, which is the property that makes a missing filter a non-event rather than a breach.

## The frontend

The frontend was TypeScript and React, and its defining technical property was that its types were generated from the same GraphQL, the graph query language, schema as the backend. The applications used React eighteen, React Router, and Apollo Client, with the Ant Design component system, which suits dense operational forms and tables far better than a consumer component kit, and Emotion for component-scoped styles. Type and hook generation used the GraphQL code generator with the typescript, typescript-operations, and typescript-react-apollo plugins, run against the shared schema plus the operation documents, producing a typed hook per operation, so a screen consumed the API, the application programming interface, through generated typed functions rather than hand-written requests. The default fetch policy was deliberately no-cache for operational reads, because in software where an operator acts on live orders a confidently stale cached read is worse than a brief loading state. The shared workspace packages were the structural backbone. A validations package held one implementation each of rules like a valid United Kingdom phone number and a valid service identifier. A hooks package held cross-application hooks. A user interface package wrapped the component system with consistent theming and layout primitives. A utilities package held shared helpers, including the function that extracted a field name from a GraphQL error path. A constants package held the error-code enumeration. The point was singular ownership, exactly one phone-number validator and one error-code enumeration imported by both frontends rather than two that drift apart. I did concrete consolidation work here. Icons had been imported from several libraries in several inconsistent ways, which both inflated the JavaScript bundle the browser downloaded and made the interface visually inconsistent, so I built one icon map exporting every icon under one name each and migrated more than twenty components to reference it, collapsing many import paths into one bundle cost and one visual language. Layout had the same problem, the same flex container with the same gap rewritten by hand in dozens of components, so I extracted small named layout utilities, a flex-gap helper and a header-row helper, and replaced the duplication with them. There were also smaller shared hooks that raised the floor for everyone building screens, a user-activity tracker, disclosure-state hooks for modals and drawers, a colour-scheme detector, and the form error handler that the next chapter is about. None of these is individually large. Their value is that when a recurring need has exactly one tested implementation, every new screen built on top of it inherits consistency automatically. A new engineer then has one correct way to do the common thing rather than several archaeological layers to study. That is the difference between a frontend that gets more consistent as it grows and one that gets more random with every feature. The code-generator configuration is worth stating because it is the frontend half of the schema-first contract. It read the shared schema plus the operation documents, ran the three plugins, kept enumeration value names rather than rewriting their casing so they matched the backend exactly, set the default fetch policy to no-cache for operational reads, and formatted the output so the generated file was reviewable rather than noise. The consequence at a call site was that a screen called a generated hook whose variables argument was the generated input type and whose result was the generated result type, so a backend schema change surfaced as a type error in the screen rather than as a wrong shape at runtime. The error-path utility lived in the shared utilities package and did exactly one thing. It took an Apollo error, read the first error's path array, and returned the last segment as the field name, which is the small primitive that made server-driven field errors possible everywhere rather than reimplemented per form. The pattern across all of it is one tested implementation per concept imported by both frontends, so consistency is inherited by construction rather than maintained by review.

## The validation framework

The form and validation framework is the subsystem I owned most completely, so I can describe its exact mechanism. The product is, from the operator's seat, a very large set of forms, and a rule that is wrong is not cosmetic. A too-strict rule blocks a real revenue-bearing order. A too-loose rule admits data that fails far later inside a carrier call. The framework combined React Hook Form for form state and submission with Zod for schema description. Each form defined one Zod schema. From that single schema we derived both the runtime validation and the static TypeScript type of the form values, through the schema library's type inference, so the validation and the type could not silently disagree because both came from one source. Getting there was an incremental migration across more than fifty forms, from ad hoc imperative rules to declarative schemas, without breaking live workflows. Underneath that, I led two dependency migrations while the framework was in daily use. The first moved the schema library from its third major version to its fourth, where the authoring interface changed. The second moved the resolver bridge between the schema library and the form library from its third major version to its fifth. Both touched essentially every form, so both were driven by the type checker and the end-to-end suite rather than by manual clicking. The technically interesting part is error binding. A server can reject input the client believed valid, a duplicate value being the canonical case, and the failure of most form systems is showing that as a generic notification with no indication of which field is wrong. The shared error-handler hook took an Apollo error, read the first error, and extracted its structured extensions code and its path. It used a small utility that returned the last segment of that path as the field name. If the code was the duplicate code, it called the form library's set-error on exactly that field with a specific message and also surfaced a notification. Otherwise it set a manual error with the server message, and it degraded gracefully when it could not localise. The result was that a backend rejection became a precise message under the one input that caused it. The field name was not a hand-typed string. It was derived from the generated input type, so a renamed schema field produced a compile error at every form referencing it rather than a silent failure. The cross-field rules used the schema library's refine mechanism, which evaluates several fields together and attaches the error to a chosen path. One real example is an amend-order schema whose refine required that either an email or a phone or a full appointment was present, attaching the error to a synthetic path so the message rendered in the right place. That refine encoded the same intent as the backend validate directives, so the same business rule existed on both sides, expressed in each language's idiom, generated and checked rather than duplicated by memory. One concrete migration detail shows why these upgrades were surgery rather than a version bump. The third to fourth major version changed the authoring interface, so every schema object had to be rewritten to the new form. Because the form values type was inferred from the schema, a wrong rewrite did not fail loudly, it changed an inferred type silently, so the only reliable safety net was the type checker compiling the consuming form plus the end-to-end suite exercising the submit path. The resolver bridge upgrade changed how the schema connected to the form library, so the integration point at every form changed at once. The error binding was the highest-value piece because it sat exactly at the backend boundary. Because the duplicate case is the single most common server-side rejection in create-heavy software, getting that one path precise removed a large, recurring source of operator confusion across every form in the product.

## Subscribers and named contacts

The subscriber and named-contact domain is the clearest single example of one rule reaching through every layer, so I will trace it concretely. A subscriber is the customer on an order. A named contact is an authorised representative tied to a subscriber. The hard rule was identity. A residential customer has a personal name and no company. A business customer has a company name and often no single personal name. The system could not require both, because a residential customer has no company, and could not require neither, because then an order is attached to nobody. The rule was that either a subscriber name or a company name must be present, and the exact behaviour differed by context, because relaxing a required field on the edit path must not retroactively invalidate records that were valid under the stricter create-time rule. That single rule was implemented in three places that had to agree. On the frontend, the Zod schema used a refine that inspected the name and company fields together and, when both were empty, attached the validation error to both fields so the operator saw exactly what was needed rather than guessing. On the backend, the GraphQL, the graph query language, input carried validate directives so a malformed or incomplete request was rejected at the boundary regardless of client behaviour, because the client is never the only line of defence. And the resulting structured error had to travel back through the shared error-handler hook to the exact frontend field, which is why the error path and extensions code mattered so much in the previous chapter. I made a deliberate series of changes here. I relaxed subscriber validation to allow genuinely optional fields where the historical rules were too strict and were blocking legitimate orders. I scoped the name-or-company requirement so that only one of subscriber name or company name was mandatory on the edit path specifically, rather than over-constraining edits and invalidating existing valid data. Each commit is small read alone. Together they are a complete conditional-validation implementation, the same rule expressed as a frontend refine and as backend directives, generated types keeping the field names honest on both sides, and a structured error carrying a code and a path so the rejection lands on the right input. The transferable point is precise. The difficulty in real validation is rarely the regular expression. It is modelling a rule that depends on other fields and on context, expressing that same rule in two languages without the definitions diverging, and routing the resulting error to the exact field with enough structure that the interface can place it. The only durable way to keep the two definitions from diverging is to derive the shared parts, the types and the codes, from one source rather than to maintain them by discipline. The refine mechanism is worth describing exactly because it is how a cross-field rule is expressed without a side channel. The refine takes a predicate over the whole parsed object and a configuration that includes the path the error should attach to, so the rule sees every field at once and the failure renders where the form expects it. In the amend-order schema the refine required that at least one of an email, a phone, or a complete appointment, meaning both an around-date and a selected appointment identifier, was present, and it attached the failure to a synthetic path so the message rendered in the right region rather than on an unrelated field. The subscriber rule used the same shape, a predicate over the personal name and the company name attaching to both fields when both were empty. The backend counterpart was the validate directive set on the input, so the boundary rejected the same incomplete input regardless of client behaviour. The two definitions did not share code, because one is a frontend predicate and one is a schema annotation, but they did share the generated input field names and the shared error-code enumeration, so the parts that would silently rot if duplicated were derived rather than retyped, and the parts that genuinely differ were each idiomatic to their side. That separation, derive what must agree and let the rest be idiomatic, is the reusable lesson.

## Performance and type safety

Two technical campaigns ran through years of commits, and both are about moving correctness from runtime to a place that fails earlier. The performance one is the event tables. Several screens render long lists of network and reporting events, and in real tenant data those lists are large. The original implementation fetched the full list and filtered and sorted it in the browser, which is acceptable for hundreds of rows and collapses at thousands, because the browser must transfer the whole dataset, hold it in memory, and sort it on the main thread, freezing the interface. The fix was to push filtering and sorting into the resolvers. The list query parameters gained a limit, a search term, and a sort specification. The resolver applied them against the store where the data already lived and where indexes exist, and the frontend received only the page it rendered. There was a specific change to sort an event subject list in the resolver rather than on the client for the same reason. The principle is that work belongs where the data is, and shipping a large dataset to a browser to discard most of it is almost always the wrong design. The type-safety campaign targeted the escape-hatch any type, which disables TypeScript checking wherever it appears. The lever was the generated types. Because the GraphQL, the graph query language, schema generated TypeScript types, I refactored forms and components to consume the generated input and result types instead of loosely shaped objects, so a future backend schema change broke the frontend build at the precise call site rather than failing silently at runtime in front of a customer. The campaign was many small commits, strongly typing form input names so a typo could not compile, replacing restated shapes with generated ones, and then fixing the genuine defects that surfaced the moment checking was actually enabled, because removing an any almost always exposes a real bug that was hiding behind it. There was also a structural readability change I made deliberately, replacing nested permission conditionals in components with an early-return authorization guard, where a component lacking permission returns nothing at the top and the remainder is the unconditional path, which makes the rendered case obvious and removes a class of conditional bug. The unifying mechanism across both campaigns is the same one that runs through the whole system. Put the work where the data is so the database does the heavy operation, and tie the types to the generated schema so the compiler, not the customer, is the one who finds the mismatch. Done continuously in small commits neither is a heroic project, and deferred indefinitely both become the reason a once-fast product is the slow one and nobody can say when it happened. It is worth being precise about the pushdown because the parameter design is the interesting part. The query gained a limit, a search term, and a sort specification, and the resolver translated those into a bounded store query rather than fetching all rows, so the network payload and the browser memory were both proportional to the page size rather than to the tenant's total event count. The sort moved server side specifically because a client sort requires the full set in memory to be correct, whereas a store sort uses an index, so moving it was not a micro-optimisation, it changed the asymptotic behaviour of the screen. On the type-safety side the lever was that the generated types were the same types the backend produced, so consuming them was not adding annotations for their own sake, it was making the frontend fail at compile time on exactly the schema changes that would otherwise fail at runtime. The early-return guard mattered for a different reason, correctness through readability, because a component whose first lines return nothing when permission is absent has an unconditional remainder, which removes the class of bug where a deeply nested permission conditional is subtly wrong. All three are the same move at different layers, make the failing case structural and early rather than incidental and late, which is the same principle the directives and the generated contracts apply on the backend.

## Quality and security

The last technical area is testing and security, described as specific mechanisms rather than as virtue. The end-to-end suite ran on Playwright and drove a real browser through complete journeys, create and activate a service, manage a subscriber, work a support ticket. I maintained that suite through interface and authentication refactors and wrote the project's internal best-practices guide for it, roughly twenty patterns and twenty anti-patterns, because a flaky suite trains a team to disbelieve a failing result, and once a team disbelieves red the suite has stopped doing its only job. Beneath it were Go fuzz tests driving malformed input into parsers, and integration tests that stood real dependencies up in containers rather than mocking them into a fiction that always passes. The security work was concrete and I can name the mechanisms. I closed a path-traversal vulnerability in the document generation tool. The output directory was resolved with the absolute-path function, the target file was joined onto it, and the code rejected any joined path that did not still begin with that resolved directory prefix, so a crafted filename could not escape the intended directory before the file handle was opened. I introduced a shared secure-file-permission constant set to an owner-only permission mode, octal six hundred, applied where files were written, addressing the weakness class for overly permissive file permissions, the common weakness enumeration entry seven three two. I coordinated dependency upgrades across the monorepo when published vulnerabilities landed in libraries we used, including raising the browser automation framework specifically to clear a known advisory, with a vulnerability scanner running in continuous integration so a vulnerable transitive dependency failed the pipeline rather than shipping. Observability was part of the same discipline. Tracing was registered at process start through OpenTelemetry and exported to the agent host. A status handler registered metrics on a separate port for scraping. And structured logging carried context, so a slow or failing request could be followed across the portal interface and the addressing service instead of being reconstructed from disconnected logs. The continuous integration pipeline enforced all of this as independent gates, container-image lint, the Go linter, the test job with the race detector enabled, the vulnerability scan, and automatic semantic versioning on the main branch, so merging was the agreement of independent automated checks rather than one person's confidence. The path-traversal fix is worth restating exactly because it is a small, checkable mechanism. The output directory was resolved to an absolute path. The target file was joined onto it. The code rejected the operation when the resulting path did not still begin with that resolved directory, so a filename containing parent-directory segments could not escape. I also pinned the output filename to a constant, removing filename injection as a separate vector. The secure-file-permission constant was a single shared value, applied at the write sites that previously used a broader mode, including a carrier specification preprocessor, the document generation tool, and a formatting tool, so the weakness class was closed in one shared place rather than per call site. The dependency hygiene was specific too. The browser automation framework was raised to clear a published advisory. An input-validation library and a build-time path-expansion dependency were bumped for their own advisories. A bundler dependency was overridden. The module-graph vulnerability scanner ran on every commit, so a vulnerable transitive dependency, not only a direct one, failed the pipeline. The Go linter ran with a long timeout so it analysed the whole module rather than sampling, and the container-image lint ran only when a container definition changed so it was precise rather than noisy. Across nearly four years and close to five thousand commits the technical throughline of my work was moving correctness earlier. From runtime to compile time through generated types. From scattered checks to declarative directives enforced by middleware. From hand-synchronised contracts to a single generation pipeline. And from manual review to pipeline gates. That single principle, make the machine enforce the invariant so a human does not have to remember it, is the engineering judgement I would bring to the next system I build.

## What I wrote in Go

The rest of this is first person and specific, because the natural question after an architecture tour is what did you personally write, so here is exactly what I did in Go. Across the project I authored or changed code in more than four hundred commits that touched Go files, as one of the primary backend contributors rather than the only one. My Go work was not spread thinly. It clustered into a few areas I owned, a custom GraphQL, the graph query language, scalar and its sanitisation, server-side input validation directives, a validation builder for subscribers and orders, two concrete security fixes, moving a sort from the browser into PostgreSQL, and a sustained push on tests and on removing repeated query work. One organising decision is worth stating up front because it shaped a lot of the rest. I established and grew a set of small, prefixed library packages under the shared Go library directory, named with an x prefix to mark them as our cross-cutting primitives rather than business logic. There was xhtml for the safe hypertext type and its sanitisation, xvalidate for composable validators, xgql for query preload helpers, and xaws for the small amount of cloud-identity logic we needed to isolate and test. The reason I pulled these into separate packages rather than leaving them inline is the same reason the frontend had shared packages. A sanitiser or a validator that lives inline in one resolver gets copied, drifts, and becomes three subtly different implementations. One in a named package with its own tests is imported, has a single behaviour, and is fixed once. Each package I will describe was small on purpose, did one thing, and carried its own unit tests, several of them to full coverage. I touched the large generated model and client packages constantly too, because every schema change regenerated them, but I am not going to claim generated code as authored work, and I want to be precise about that distinction throughout, because the difference between code you generated and code you designed is exactly the kind of thing a good interviewer probes. What follows is the designed part.

## The HTML scalar I built

The piece of backend Go I am most willing to be questioned on is the safe hypertext scalar. The problem was concrete. Notification bodies and activity messages needed to carry limited formatting, not just plain text, which means user-influenced markup was going to be stored and later rendered in another user's browser, and that is the exact setup for cross-site scripting, the attack where injected markup runs in someone else's session. My solution was a custom GraphQL, the graph query language, scalar type, in a package I created called xhtml, with its own marshal and unmarshal functions so the type system itself carried the safety guarantee rather than leaving it to whoever wrote the resolver. On unmarshal the value was run through the bluemonday HTML sanitiser. I did not use a single blanket policy. I configured a user-generated-content policy that allowed a deliberately small set of style properties, colour, background colour, font size, margin, padding, and border, so formatting survived but scripting and dangerous attributes did not. I added a stricter links-only policy variant for contexts, like notification messages, where the only thing that should survive is a controlled anchor. I exposed a validate-with-policy entry point so the calling context chose the policy explicitly rather than getting an implicit default. The directive side lived in a second package, gqlinput, where I wrote the html directive handler that the generated schema invoked on annotated input fields, so sanitisation happened before a resolver ever saw the value. A subtle but important decision was reversing the generated client side back to plain strings, so the typed clients that other services used did not need to depend on the scalar type, and the sanitisation guarantee was enforced once, authoritatively, at the resolver boundary rather than partially in several clients. I rolled the scalar out across the notification schema and then across activity messages, which reached into dozens of resolver files because activity is created from many places. I also fixed a real defect I had shipped, where a trailing newline coming from a text area input slipped past a check, by trimming before validation, which is the kind of bug you only find from the field and exactly why the type carried tests. The reason this is the work I would lead with is that it is a clean example of moving a security property from something a developer must remember into something the type system and a directive enforce by default.

## My server side validation

The second area was server-side input validation expressed as a GraphQL, the graph query language, directive rather than as imperative checks inside resolvers. The motivating case was search. Several list queries took a search parameter, and an empty search string is not the same as no search. An empty string is a client bug that should be rejected at the boundary, while a missing value is legitimate and means do not filter. I added a validate directive with a tag combining optional-if-empty and a greater-than-zero length rule onto the search field of the subscriber list parameters and then the event list parameters, which cover events and network events. The mechanism is worth being precise about because it is the part an interviewer would push on. The schema-first generator emits the input unmarshalling code, and because the field carried the directive, the generated unmarshal path calls the validate directive with the tag string before the value is assigned into the input struct, so an invalid value is rejected before any resolver logic runs and before it can reach the data layer. The validation itself is struct-tag based, the same style as the widely used Go validator library, so the rule is declarative data on the schema field rather than a branch I had to write and remember in each resolver. I backed this with integration tests that asserted the two distinct behaviours explicitly. An empty string is rejected with a validation error. A nil, meaning the parameter was simply omitted, is accepted and means no filter. That pair of tests matters more than it looks, because the entire point of the change is the distinction between absent and empty, and a test suite that does not pin both halves of that distinction would let a future change quietly collapse them. This is a small feature by line count and a representative one by philosophy, the same philosophy as the directives chapter earlier, push the rule to the boundary, express it as data on the schema, and let the generated code enforce it so a new query that reuses the parameter type inherits the validation for free rather than having to re-implement it correctly.

## The xvalidate subscriber rules

The third area was the validation builder for subscribers and service orders, which is where I owned a genuinely tricky piece of domain logic in Go. The validation here could not be a flat list of required fields, because the correctness depended on context, and getting it wrong had direct commercial cost, too strict and a legitimate order is blocked, too loose and a broken order fails later inside a carrier interaction. I worked in a package I will call the validation builder, xvalidate, which exposed a composable builder, a new subscriber validator onto which individual rules were chained, with address, with first name, with last name, with email, with phone, and a whitelisted email domain rule that took its allowed domains from configuration rather than hard-coding them. The builder shape mattered because it let the rule set be assembled per context instead of being one fixed function. The specific change I am describing is one where I deliberately relaxed subscriber validation to make several fields genuinely optional. The historical rules required an address and personal name fields that were, in reality, not always available at the point an order was created, and that strictness was rejecting legitimate orders. I removed those chained requirements from the validator used by the new-service-order validation activity, while deliberately keeping the whitelisted email domain rule, because that one is a real business constraint rather than an over-tightening. Critically I updated the test suite to match, removing the cases that asserted the old, too-strict behaviour, for example the case that demanded an address and the case that rejected a non-whitelisted email when email itself was now optional. I want to be explicit that deleting tests is normally a smell, and here it was the correct move precisely because the tests encoded a requirement we had decided was wrong, and leaving them would have meant the suite was now pinning behaviour the product no longer wanted. This pairs directly with the subscribers chapter from the architecture section, where the same name-or-company rule had a frontend half. This is the server half, in Go, at the task and activity layer, enforced regardless of what any client sent, because the client is never the only line of defence.

## Two Go security fixes

The fourth area is two specific security fixes in Go that I can describe down to the mechanism, because vague claims about security are worthless and specific ones are checkable. The first was a path-traversal vulnerability in a document-generation tool. The tool wrote a generated file into an output directory, and the output path was assembled in a way where a crafted directory value containing parent-directory segments could cause the write to land outside the intended directory, which is the classic traversal weakness, the common weakness enumeration entry numbered twenty-two. My fix resolved the output directory to an absolute path, joined the target filename onto that absolute base, and then explicitly rejected the operation, failing hard, when the resulting path did not still begin with the resolved base directory, so an escape was caught before any file handle was opened. I also pinned the output filename to a constant rather than letting it be influenced by input, removing filename injection as a separate vector, and I added a focused test file that drove the actual traversal payloads, parent segments aimed at temporary and system directories, and asserted they were rejected. The second fix was file permissions. Several tools wrote files with a broad permission mode that allowed group and other read access on content that should not have it, which is the weakness class for overly permissive permissions, the entry numbered seven hundred and thirty-two. I introduced a single shared constant in a file-parser library package, set to an owner-only read and write mode, octal six hundred, and applied it at the write sites that had been permissive, the document-generation tool, a formatting tool, and a specification preprocessor. The detail that makes this a good fix rather than a one-off patch is that it was one shared constant, so the secure default became importable and consistent rather than re-decided, correctly or not, at each call site. Neither fix is large. Both are the kind of change that does not exist on any feature board and is exactly the difference between a tool you can run against real data and one you should not.

## Sorting moved into Postgres

The fifth area is a performance and correctness change with a satisfying shape, moving address sorting out of the browser and into PostgreSQL. The original design fetched addresses and sorted them on the frontend, which has two problems. It is slow and memory-heavy once a postcode returns many addresses. And, more interestingly, it was sorting them lexically, so building number two sorted after building number ten, which is wrong to a human reading an address list. I refactored the addressing service handler, which spoke gRPC, the remote procedure call framework. I changed a function that had been returning a slice of addresses into one that returned only an error and instead populated state, and I changed an intermediate map from carrying full address rows to being a set that tracked keys only, which removed redundant copying along the hydration path. The substantive part was threading sort and order parameters down into the database query. The query layer was generated by the typed SQL, structured query language, tool from an annotated query file, so I added the sort into that query, and the natural numeric ordering was done in the database using a regular-expression match to extract the leading numeric portion of the building number and order by that as a number, so two correctly precedes ten. Pushing the sort into the database is the right move for the reason I gave in the performance chapter. The database already holds the data and has indexes, and shipping the whole set to the browser to reorder it is wasted transfer and wasted main-thread time. I deleted the now-dead frontend sort utility as part of the same change, because a fix that leaves the superseded code in place is only half a fix and invites the old path back. I backed the handler with a substantial test, a few hundred lines, covering the sort scenarios specifically, because a sort is exactly the kind of logic that looks right and is subtly wrong at the boundaries, empty input, a single item, equal building numbers, and missing numeric prefixes, and an untested sort is a latent bug with a long fuse.

## N plus one and tests

The last area covers the work that has no screen at all, query efficiency and test coverage, which together were a large share of my Go commits. On efficiency, list endpoints had the classic N plus one query problem, where rendering a list of subscribers or product offerings issued one query for the list and then one more query per row for a related entity, so a page of fifty rows became fifty-one round trips. I added preload helpers in a small package I created, xgql, that let a resolver declare the related entities it would need so they were fetched in a bounded number of queries instead of one per row. I applied that to the subscriber list and the product offering list, colocating the GraphQL, the graph query language, fragments so the frontend asked for exactly what the preload satisfied. That is the same put-the-work-where-the-data-is principle as the sorting change, applied to read amplification rather than to ordering. On testing, I drove a deliberate coverage push across the small shared Go libraries, bringing packages for error codes, mime handling, the NATS, the messaging system, JSON helper, the activity helper, and a connection-key helper to full statement coverage. I also removed one flaky test rather than leave it eroding trust, because a test that fails at random trains people to ignore failures and is worse than no test. I wrote a large body of edge-case tests for the subscriber-profile deletion flow, several hundred lines, covering the parts most likely to be wrong under failure, the event publishing, the network cleanup, and the backup-and-restore path, because a deletion flow is precisely where partial failure does the most damage. I also extracted the cloud identity pool name matching into a small package with its own tests, so logic that had been buried in a tenant flow became independently testable, and I added deterministic seed data for batch-order integration tests so those tests asserted against a fixed world rather than an incidental one. None of this is glamorous and all of it is why the system could be changed quickly without fear, which, after nearly four years in this codebase, is the single property I would most want a new team to know I can build and defend, in Go or anywhere else.
